A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MENTOR and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. The original material can be matched across reformatting, relocation and the additional supplementary studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation learning curves, gradient and expert-use analyses, and real-world robotic success rates and timing measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds component ablations, sensitivity tests, multitask experiments, gradient measurements and a disturbance demonstration.

M1.justification: The MoE policy, top-k routing, entropy-based load-balancing loss and Gaussian perturbation distribution maintained from top-performing agents remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 are reformatted without changing their procedures.

E1.justification: The original benchmarks and physical tasks remain. Appendix G extends the existing Meta-World MT5 coverage with MT3, MT4 and MT7 combinations, adding faucet, plate-sliding, button-press and peg-insertion tasks. Appendix I adds Assembly evaluation with target relocation. These extend existing manipulation scenarios.

E2.justification: DrM, DrQ-v2, ALIX and TACO remain the external baselines. Appendix C newly includes MENTOR w/o TP, retaining MoE but using random perturbation, in component comparisons. This adds a comparison variant absent from v1's ablations without introducing a new external baseline family.

E3.justification: The original benchmark and robot protocols are retained, but supplementary evaluation design expands substantially. New protocols include crossed component controls, expert-count/top-k sweeps, matched-performance normalized training times, multitask MoE-versus-MLP training with perturbation disabled, and evaluation-time relocation of the Assembly pillar.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's perturbation illustration, expert-use studies and real-world ablations, v2 adds four-task component ablations, MoE hyperparameter sensitivity, single-task stage-pair gradient analysis, multitask scaling comparisons and an Assembly disturbance case study. These substantially broaden tests of contribution attribution, mechanism and robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions specify four simulation seeds and retain Figure 6's standard-deviation shading for DMC and success-rate ranges for Meta-World and Adroit. The new component ablations explicitly reuse the same four seeds; no increased run count or new statistical estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: The original benchmark, robotic success and timing results are retained, while substantial supplementary results are added. For example, v2 Table 2 reports Hopper Hop normalized training times of 0.6167 for MENTOR, 1 for w/o TP and 0.85 for w/o MoE. New sensitivity, multitask, gradient and disturbance findings supplement these results.

T1.justification: Appendix C introduces a mathematical definition of normalized efficiency: training time divided by the maximum of three matched-performance training times. Existing MoE, dormant-neuron, load-balancing and reward equations remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The two central contributions and claims of superior sample efficiency remain the same. Both versions retain the headline real-world success comparison of 83% versus 32%. The additional appendix evidence supports these existing claims.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds a concrete explanation of conflicting Assembly objectives: reaching to grasp can increase distance from the target pillar. v2 also interprets expert-count sensitivity and component complementarity, and its conclusion adds limitations concerning scaling to many tasks and diverse robot embodiments.

D1.justification: The appendix video-access link changes to the mentor-vrl site. Core reproducibility information—including the hyperparameter table, RTX 3090 hardware, camera observations, action spaces, reward functions and automatic resets—is preserved.

R1.justification: The cited works and positioning relative to visual RL, MoE and network perturbation research remain unchanged. Bibliographic reformatting and the exchanged Laskin 2020a/2020b suffixes refer to the same underlying papers.

P1.justification: The abstract, preliminaries, several method and experiment passages, and conclusion undergo substantial condensation or rewriting. The real-world training-time discussion moves into Appendix E, and the appendix narrative is reorganized around separate validation sections. Author affiliations and correspondence information also change.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column ICML layout throughout, resizes and relocates displays, and reformats pseudocode. It adds five analysis figures and a normalized training-time table, revises captions and benchmark labels, and relocates v1's timing Figure 8 as Figure 14.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens component attribution through four-task ablations (Figure 9 and Table 2) and supports the single-task gradient-conflict explanation with direct measurements (Figure 13). Sensitivity and multitask tests provide further useful validation while preserving the original evidence. These incrementally strengthen already supported conclusions; the new disturbance test remains a qualitative demonstration.
